lessons.title: Supersaturation and Nucleation
lessons.body:
Supersaturation is the driving force for sugar crystallization. It measures how much sugar is dissolved beyond the equilibrium saturation point at a given temperature. In practice, you create supersaturation by evaporating water or cooling a sugar solution. The supersaturation coefficient (S) is the ratio of sugar to water in the solution divided by the same ratio at saturation. For crystallization to occur, S must be above 1.0. But if S goes too high, you get unwanted spontaneous nucleation â tiny crystals that ruin your product.

In African sugar factories, pan boilers control supersaturation by adjusting vacuum, steam pressure, and feed rates. A typical target for crystal growth is S between 1.2 and 1.4. At S below 1.1, crystals barely grow. Above 1.5, you risk nucleation and false grain. Use a refractometer or a microwave moisture analyzer to check dissolved solids (Brix) and temperature to calculate S. For example, at 70Â°C, a saturated sucrose solution is about 76% solids. If your pan has 80% solids at 70Â°C, S = (80/20) / (76/24) = 4.0/3.17 = 1.26 â good for growth.

Nucleation is the birth of new crystals. You want controlled nucleation only when starting a strike. In batch pans, you introduce seed crystals (slurry of fine sugar in alcohol) at the right moment. Alternatively, you can nucleate by shocking the syrup â dropping temperature or adding a small amount of powdered sugar. In continuous pans, nucleation happens naturally but must be balanced with growth to maintain crystal size.

Practical tip: Keep your pan clean. Scale and burnt sugar act as nucleation sites, causing fine grain. In many African factories, pan boiling is still manual â watch the sight glass and feel the consistency. A drop of massecuite on a glass slide, viewed under a simple magnifier, shows crystal size. If you see many tiny crystals, reduce supersaturation by adding water or syrup. If crystals are few and large, increase evaporation. This hands-on skill is learned on the job.

Remember, supersaturation and nucleation are the heart of sugar boiling. Master them, and you control crystal size, yield, and molasses exhaustion. Poor control means lost sugar in molasses and poor quality.

lessons.title: Crystallization Methods: Batch and Continuous
lessons.body:
Sugar crystallization is done in vacuum pans. There are two main methods: batch and continuous. Batch pans are the traditional choice in many African sugar mills. They work in cycles: fill, concentrate, seed, grow, and discharge. A batch pan might take 2â4 hours per strike. You start by pulling a vacuum (around 600â650 mmHg) and feeding clarified syrup. As water evaporates, supersaturation rises. When you reach S=1.2â1.3, you add seed crystals or nucleate. Then you feed more syrup to grow crystals while maintaining supersaturation. Finally, you drop the massecuite (mixture of crystals and mother liquor) to a receiver.

Continuous pans are becoming more common, especially in larger factories. They have multiple compartments. Massecuite flows from one end to the other, with syrup feed and steam heating in each section. Continuous pans run 24/7, producing a steady stream of massecuite. They are more energy-efficient and easier to automate, but they require careful control to avoid fine grain. In Africa, continuous pans are found in countries like South Africa, Egypt, and Mauritius. Smaller mills often stick to batch because they are simpler and cheaper to maintain.

Which method to choose? Batch pans are flexible â you can adjust for different sugar qualities (white, raw, soft). They are ideal for small-scale operations. Continuous pans need a steady supply of syrup and skilled operators. They give consistent crystal size but are less forgiving of fluctuations.

Key parameters for both: vacuum, temperature (around 65â75Â°C), and supersaturation. You also need to control the rate of syrup addition. Too fast, and you create new crystals (nucleation). Too slow, and crystals stop growing. In batch pans, you use a

â a starting volume of syrup â then build on it. In continuous pans, you maintain a constant level and density.

For a learner in a rural African setting, start with batch pans. Learn to read the massecuite: it should feel like thick honey. A simple test: take a sample, cool it, and rub between fingers â you should feel grains, not a smooth paste. If smooth, you have too much fine grain. Adjust by adding more seed or slowing feed. With practice, you can produce good crystals without expensive instruments.

lessons.title: Centrifugal Separation of Crystals and Molasses
lessons.body: After crystallization, you have massecuite â a mix of sugar crystals and molasses. To separate them, you use centrifugals. These are machines that spin at high speed, using centrifugal force to throw the heavy molasses through a screen while retaining sugar crystals. In African sugar factories, you'll find batch centrifugals (often called

) and continuous centrifugals.

Batch centrifugals are common in small to medium mills. They work in cycles: load, spin, wash, unload. A typical cycle takes 3â5 minutes. You load about 500â800 kg of massecuite into a basket lined with a fine screen (0.06â0.08 mm openings). The basket spins at 1000â1800 rpm. Molasses flies out through the screen, and crystals stay inside. After spinning for 1â2 minutes, you spray water or steam to wash the crystal surface, removing remaining molasses. Then you spin again to dry, and finally unload the sugar.

Continuous centrifugals are used for low-grade massecuite (final molasses). They have a conical basket and operate continuously. They are more efficient for high-volume, low-purity work. But for high-grade sugar (white or raw), batch centrifugals give better washing and lower color.

Key controls: spin speed, screen condition, and wash water. If the screen is torn, crystals escape with molasses â lost sugar. If you use too much wash water, you dissolve crystals and increase molasses purity. A good rule: wash with 3â5% water by weight of massecuite. In many African factories, operators judge by sight: the sugar should look bright, not sticky. If it's sticky, increase spin time or wash.

Safety is critical. Centrifugals are heavy and fast. Never open the cover while spinning. Ensure the basket is balanced â uneven loads cause vibration and can damage the machine. After unloading, check the screen for holes. Replace worn screens promptly.

For a small-scale processor, a manual batch centrifugal might be affordable. But even a simple basket centrifuge can work: line a drum with cloth, spin it with a motor, and you can separate small batches. The principle is the same. The goal is to get clean crystals and molasses that can be further processed or sold.

lessons.title: Affination and Washing of Raw Sugar
lessons.body:
Raw sugar from centrifugals still has a thin film of molasses on the crystal surface. This film contains impurities, color, and ash. To produce white sugar, you must remove it. Affination is the process of mixing raw sugar with a heavy syrup (affination syrup) to soften the molasses film, then centrifuging to wash it off. It's like a pre-wash before refining.

In African refineries, affination is done in a mingler â a horizontal trough with paddles. Raw sugar and affination syrup (about 70â75 Brix) are mixed for 5â10 minutes. The syrup dissolves the molasses coating. The mixture, called magma, is then fed to centrifugals. There, it is spun and washed with water. The washed sugar (affined sugar) has lower color and purity, ready for melting and further processing. The separated syrup (affination syrup) is recycled or used for molasses production.

If you don't have a refinery, you can still improve raw sugar quality by simple washing. In a batch centrifugal, after spinning off the main molasses, spray water directly onto the crystal bed. Use about 5â10% water by weight of sugar. Spin again to remove the wash water. This reduces surface molasses and improves sugar quality. But be careful: too much water dissolves sugar, reducing yield. In small-scale operations, a simple technique is to wash raw sugar in a drum with a small amount of hot water (60â70Â°C), stir, and then filter or centrifuge. The wash water becomes a sweet syrup that can be reused.

Why affinate? Because raw sugar with high molasses film causes problems in refining: it increases color, ash, and refining costs. Affination reduces these by 50â70%. For direct consumption raw sugar (like in some African markets), a light wash is enough.

Practical tips: Use clean water. If water is hard, soften it or use condensate. Control temperature â too hot dissolves crystals, too cold doesn't remove molasses. Aim for 60â70Â°C. Check the color of the wash water: it should go from dark to light. When it runs clear, stop washing. In many African factories, affination is a manual job â workers judge by eye. With training, you can produce better sugar for local markets.

lessons.title: Molasses Recovery and Utilization
lessons.body:
Final molasses is the heavy, dark syrup left after all recoverable sugar has been crystallized. It typically contains 45â55% sucrose, 10â20% reducing sugars, and 5â10% ash. In African sugar factories, molasses is a valuable by-product. Recovering it efficiently means maximizing sugar extraction and finding profitable uses.

Recovery starts with exhausting the molasses â getting as much sugar out as possible. This is done by boiling the molasses to a higher concentration (around 85â90 Brix) and crystallizing again. The resulting sugar (called final molasses sugar or C-sugar) is low purity and often sent back to the affination stage. The remaining molasses is then centrifuged off. In many factories, this is done in continuous centrifugals. The key is to control supersaturation and temperature. If you over-boil, you get viscous molasses that won't crystallize. If under-boil, you leave sugar in molasses.

Utilization of molasses in Africa is diverse. The most common uses:
1. Animal feed: Molasses is mixed with roughage (like maize stover or bagasse) to make nutritious feed for cattle. It provides energy and improves palatability. A typical mix: 10â20% molasses, 80â90% roughage.
2. Ethanol production: Many African countries (e.g., Kenya, South Africa, Malawi) ferment molasses to produce ethanol for fuel or beverages. A tonne of molasses yields about 250â300 liters of ethanol.
3. Food and beverage: In some cultures, molasses is used in baking (gingerbread, cookies) or as a sweetener. It's also used to make traditional alcoholic drinks like mowin in Nigeria or muratina in Kenya.
4. Fertilizer: Molasses can be composted or applied directly to soil as a carbon source for microbes. It's also used in bio-fertilizer production.
5. Other industrial uses: Citric acid, yeast, and vinegar production.

For small-scale processors, selling molasses to local farmers for animal feed is often the easiest. You can also use it to make silage. To store molasses, keep it in sealed drums or tanks away from moisture. It can last for months. If you want to add value, consider small-scale ethanol distillation â but that requires licenses and safety measures.

Recovering more sugar from molasses reduces waste and increases profits. Even a 1% increase in molasses exhaustion can mean significant extra income for a factory. So pay attention to boiling and centrifugation â every crystal counts.

lessons.title: Crystal Size Distribution and Quality Control
lessons.body:
Crystal size distribution (CSD) is the range of crystal sizes in a sugar sample. It affects centrifugation, washing, and final product quality. A good CSD means most crystals are within a narrow size range â uniform crystals. Poor CSD means many fine and coarse crystals mixed. In African sugar factories, CSD is controlled by crystallization and centrifugation.

Why does CSD matter? Uniform crystals centrifuge better: molasses drains evenly, washing is efficient, and sugar dries faster. Non-uniform crystals cause problems: fines clog screens, coarse crystals trap molasses, and you get inconsistent color. Also, buyers prefer uniform crystals â they look better and dissolve predictably.

How to measure CSD? In a lab, you use a set of sieves (e.g., 0.5 mm, 0.8 mm, 1.0 mm, 1.2 mm). You weigh 100 g of sugar, shake through sieves for 5â10 minutes, and weigh the fraction on each sieve. Plot the results. A good white sugar might have 80% between 0.6 and 1.0 mm. For raw sugar, larger crystals (1.0â1.5 mm) are common. In the field, you can use a simple magnifier and a ruler. Take a sample, spread on a glass, and measure 20 crystals. Calculate the average and range. If you see many tiny crystals (fines) or huge ones, adjust your pan boiling.

Quality control also includes moisture, color, and ash. Moisture should be below 0.05% for white sugar, 0.1â0.2% for raw. Color is measured in ICUMSA units â white sugar under 45, raw up to 2000. Ash indicates mineral content. In small operations, you can check moisture by drying a sample in an oven at 105Â°C for 3 hours. Color by comparing to a standard chart.

To improve CSD, control nucleation and growth. In batch pans, seed with a uniform slurry. Avoid temperature shocks. In centrifugals, use the right screen and spin speed. If you have many fines, reduce supersaturation or add more seed. If crystals are too large, increase nucleation slightly.

Record your data. Keep a log of pan boiling times, temperatures, and CSD results. Over time, you'll see patterns. In many African factories, simple record-keeping has improved sugar quality by 10â20%. Train your operators to spot problems early. Quality control is not just for labs â it's for everyone on the floor.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Crystallization and Centrifugation in African Sugar Processing

This practical reference consolidates the operating knowledge that pan boilers, centrifuge operators, and quality controllers need on a daily basis in African sugar factories. Whether you are running a 1,500 TCD (tonnes cane per day) plant in Uganda, a 6,000 TCD factory in Eswatini, or a refinery attached to a Kenyan mill, the underlying physics of supersaturation, nucleation, crystal growth, and centrifugal separation is the same. What changes is the feedstock quality, the energy cost, the labour skill mix, and the market you are selling into. This lesson is written for the person who has to make a decision on shift: adjust the vacuum pan, change the centrifuge screen, or divert a massecuite stream. It is business-first because in African sugar, every kilogram of recoverable crystal and every minute of downtime has a direct effect on the factory's bottom line.

Supersaturation and Nucleation: The Control Lever

Supersaturation coefficient (S) is the ratio of the actual sucrose concentration in the mother liquor to its saturation concentration at the same temperature and purity. In practice, pan boilers work within three zones: S below 1.0 (undersaturated, crystals dissolve), S between 1.0 and 1.2 (metastable, existing crystals grow but new ones do not form), and S above 1.2 (labile, spontaneous nucleation occurs). The skill of crystallization is to hold the pan in the metastable zone for as long as possible, then deliberately raise supersaturation to seed the pan, then drop back to grow the seed evenly.

In African factories running on cane that has travelled long distances or been burnt, the non-sucrose-to-water ratio is often higher than in temperate mills. This narrows the metastable zone and makes nucleation harder to control. A boiler who has learned on high-purity A-massecuite may struggle with C-massecuite where purity can drop below 60. The practical answer is to use the refractometer and the conductivity probe together, and to trust the crystal content reading from the pan's own instrumentation rather than the clock.

The business consequence is straightforward. If you nucleate too early or too often, you create fines that pass through the centrifuge screens and end up in molasses, where you lose them. If you nucleate too late, you grow too few crystals and the massecuite becomes too viscous to centrifuge, increasing cycle times and power consumption. Both errors cost money. In a 5,000 TCD factory, a 1% improvement in crystal recovery from C-massecuite is worth roughly US$120,000â180,000 per season at typical African sugar prices.

Crystallization Methods: Batch and Continuous

Batch pans remain dominant in African raw sugar factories because they offer flexibility with variable cane quality and lower capital cost. A batch pan is charged with liquor, seeded, and boiled to a target crystal content (typically 45â55% for A-massecuite, 40â48% for B, and 35â45% for C). The operator controls vacuum, steam pressure, and feed rate to maintain supersaturation. Continuous pans, by contrast, are better suited to refineries and to factories with stable, high-purity feedstock. They run at steady state, use less steam per tonne of crystal, and produce more uniform crystal size distribution (CSD). In Africa, continuous pans are found in the larger South African and Eswatini refineries, and increasingly in Kenyan and Nigerian back-end refineries.

The practical decision rule: if your feedstock purity varies by more than 3 points week-to-week, stay batch. If your purity is stable and your energy cost is high, continuous pays back in 3â5 years through steam savings alone.

Centrifugal Separation of Crystals and Molasses

Batch centrifuges (usually 1,200â1,800 rpm basket machines) are the workhorse in raw sugar houses. The cycle is: load, spin to drain mother liquor, wash with water or steam, spin dry, plough, and discharge. Cycle time is typically 2â5 minutes for A-massecuite and 8â15 minutes for C-massecuite. Continuous centrifuges (screen or conical types) are used for low-grade massecuites where throughput matters more than crystal purity.

Key operating variables: basket speed (affects G-force and drainage), screen slot size (typically 0.06â0.12 mm), wash water quality and temperature (60â80Â°C), and plough timing. In African factories, the most common cause of high molasses purity is insufficient wash or worn screens. A worn screen lets crystals through and raises molasses purity by 2â4 points, which directly increases sugar loss.

Table 1: Typical Centrifuge Operating Parameters for African Raw Sugar Factories
Parameter A-Massecuite B-Massecuite C-Massecuite
Purity of massecuite (%) 78â82 68â74 55â64
Crystal content (%) 48â55 42â48 35â45
Cycle time (min) 2â4 4â7 8â15
Wash water (% on massecuite) 3â6 5â9 8â15
Wash water temp (Â°C) 65â80 65â80 70â85
Screen slot (mm) 0.06â0.08 0.08â0.10 0.10â0.12
Molasses purity after separation (%) 62â68 52â58 38â45

Source: Adapted from Rein, P. (2007). "Cane Sugar Engineering," Verlag Dr. Albert Bartens KG, Berlin, and from the African Sugar Technologists' Association (ASTA) 2019 Congress Proceedings, "Centrifuge Performance Benchmarking in East African Mills."

Affination and Washing of Raw Sugar

Affination is the process of mixing raw sugar with a heavy syrup (affination syrup) to soften the molasses film, then centrifuging to remove it. It is the first step in most African refineries and is increasingly used in raw sugar factories that supply direct-consumption markets. The goal is to reduce colour and ash before the raw sugar goes to the melter or the refinery. A well-run affination station can reduce raw sugar colour by 30â50% and ash by 20â40%.

Operating rules: affination syrup purity should be 2â4 points below the raw sugar purity, temperature should be 70â80Â°C, and mixing time should be 5â15 minutes. In African refineries, the most common mistake is using too little syrup, which fails to soften the molasses film, or too much, which dissolves crystal and reduces yield.

â  SAFETY WARNING: Centrifuge and Vacuum Pan Hazards

Never open a centrifuge basket while it is spinning. Even at low speed, a basket can cause fatal injury. Always wait for the plough to complete and the basket to come to a full stop before inspection. In vacuum pans, never bypass the sight glass or the pressure relief valve. Hot massecuite at 60â70Â°C can cause severe burns. In African factories where ambient temperatures often exceed 35Â°C, heat stress compounds burn risk. Ensure all operators wear heat-resistant gloves, face shields, and closed shoes. Lockout/tagout procedures must be enforced before any maintenance on centrifuges, pumps, or pan agitators. Report any unusual vibration, noise, or smell immediately â these are early signs of bearing failure or massecuite carryover.

Molasses Recovery and Utilization

Final molasses is not waste; it is a revenue stream. In Africa, molasses is sold for ethanol production (Kenya, Uganda, Malawi), animal feed (Nigeria, Tanzania), and increasingly for bioenergy and biochemicals. The recovery target is to exhaust molasses to the lowest practical purity while keeping it pumpable. Exhaustion is measured by the purity drop between C-massecuite and final molasses. A well-run factory achieves a purity drop of 18â24 points. If the drop is less than 15 points, you are losing sucrose and should review pan boiling, centrifuge wash, and molasses cooling.

Molasses storage matters. At African ambient temperatures, molasses can ferment within days if not cooled below 40Â°C and stored in closed tanks. Fermentation destroys sucrose and creates alcohol, which reduces the price you get from ethanol buyers and can cause tank corrosion.

Table 2: Typical Final Molasses Composition and Recovery Targets in African Factories
Parameter Typical Range Target / Benchmark
Sucrose content (%) 28â36 <32
Purity (%) 38â48 <42
Brix (%) 80â88 82â86
Ash (%) 8â14 <12
Purity drop (C-massecuite to molasses) 14â20 18â24
Storage temperature (Â°C) 40â55 <40
pH 5.0â6.5 5.5â6.0

Source: Adapted from the International Sugar Organization (ISO) "World Sugar Balance and Molasses Utilization Report," 2021, and from the Kenya Sugar Research Foundation (KESREF) Technical Bulletin No. 4, "Molasses Quality and Recovery in Kenyan Mills," 2019.

Crystal Size Distribution and Quality Control

Crystal size distribution (CSD) is the single best indicator of pan boiling and centrifuge performance. The target for raw sugar is a mean aperture (MA) of 0.6â0.9 mm with a coefficient of variation (CV) below 30%. A CV above 35% means you have too many fines or too many large crystals, both of which cause problems: fines increase molasses losses, and large crystals slow centrifugation and increase wash water demand.

In African factories, CSD is often measured only once per shift or less. Best practice is to measure every 4 hours using a sieve shaker or an automated image analysis system. The data should be plotted on a control chart and reviewed at the daily production meeting. If CV exceeds 35% for two consecutive shifts, the pan boiler should review seeding technique, supersaturation control, and feed rate. If MA drops below 0.5 mm, the centrifuge operator should check screen condition and wash water flow.

Quality control also covers colour (ICUMSA), ash, moisture, and safety parameters such as lead and arsenic. For export markets, African raw sugar must meet the buyer's specification, which is usually ICUMSA 800â1200 for raw and below 45 for refined. Inconsistent CSD is the most common reason for rejection of African raw sugar in EU and Middle East markets.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Check supersaturation every 15 minutes using refractometer and conductivity; keep S between 1.1 and 1.2 during growth.
  • Verify seed crystal size before charging; seed should be 0.1â0.2 mm and added as a slurry, not dry.
  • Monitor centrifuge cycle time; if A-massecuite exceeds 4 minutes, check screen condition and massecuite viscosity.
  • Test wash water temperature; keep at 65â80Â°C. Cold water increases molasses purity and sugar loss.
  • Record molasses purity after every C-centrifuge cycle; target below 42% and purity drop above 18 points.
  • Measure CSD every 4 hours; target MA 0.6â0.9 mm and CV below 30%.
  • Inspect screens daily for tears, wear, and blockage; replace any screen with slots wider than 0.12 mm.
  • Enforce lockout/tagout before any maintenance on centrifuges, pans, or pumps; never bypass safety interlocks.

Further Reading

  • South African Sugar Technologists' Association (SASTA) â Proceedings and Technical Papers (free abstracts and selected full papers on crystallization and centrifugation).
  • International Sugar Organization (ISO) â World Sugar Balance and Molasses Reports (free summaries and statistical bulletins).
  • FAO â Sugar and Bioenergy Technical Reports (free PDFs on sugar processing, molasses utilization, and African agribusiness).
  • Kenya Sugar Research Foundation (KESREF) â Technical Bulletins (free downloads on molasses quality and factory performance).
  • African Sugar Technologists' Association (ASTA) â Congress Proceedings (free abstracts and selected papers on East and Southern African factory operations).

Business takeaway: In African sugar processing, the difference between a profitable and a marginal factory is often less than 2 points of molasses purity and less than 5% CV in crystal size. Both are controllable on shift, with the right instrumentation, training, and discipline. Invest in your pan boilers and centrifuge operators, measure relentlessly, and treat molasses as a product, not a waste stream.

quiz.q: What does supersaturation measure?
options: A) The amount of sugar dissolved beyond saturation
B) The temperature of the syrup
quiz.explanation: Supersaturation is the ratio of dissolved sugar to water compared to saturation, indicating excess sugar available for crystallization.

quiz.q: What is the target supersaturation coefficient for crystal growth?
quiz.explanation: At S between 1.2 and 1.4, crystals grow well without excessive nucleation.

quiz.q: What happens if supersaturation is too high?
quiz.explanation: High supersaturation causes unwanted nucleation, creating many fine crystals.

quiz.q: Which tool can be used to check dissolved solids for supersaturation?
quiz.explanation: A refractometer measures Brix (dissolved solids), which is used with temperature to calculate supersaturation.

quiz.q: What is nucleation?
options: D) Separation of crystals from molasses
quiz.explanation: Nucleation is the birth of new crystals, either spontaneously or by seeding.

quiz.q: In batch pans, how is nucleation typically controlled?
quiz.explanation: Seeding with fine sugar crystals provides controlled nucleation sites.

quiz.q: What is a common problem if a pan has scale or burnt sugar?
quiz.explanation: Scale and burnt sugar act as nucleation sites, causing fine grain.

quiz.q: Which crystallization method is more common in small African mills?
quiz.explanation: Batch pans are simpler, cheaper, and more flexible for small-scale operations.

quiz.q: What is the typical cycle time for a batch pan strike?
quiz.explanation: A batch pan strike usually takes 2 to 4 hours from fill to discharge.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of continuous pans?
quiz.explanation: Continuous pans are easier to automate and provide steady production.

quiz.q: What is massecuite?
options: B) Mixture of crystals and mother liquor
quiz.explanation: Massecuite is the mixture of sugar crystals and molasses that comes from the pan.

quiz.q: In a batch centrifugal, what is the purpose of washing?
quiz.explanation: Washing with water or steam removes the molasses film from crystal surfaces.

quiz.q: What is a typical screen opening size for a batch centrifugal?
quiz.explanation: Fine screens of 0.06â0.08 mm retain sugar crystals while letting molasses through.

quiz.q: What happens if the centrifugal screen is torn?
quiz.explanation: Torn screens allow crystals to pass through, causing sugar loss.

quiz.q: How much wash water is typically used in a batch centrifugal?
quiz.explanation: Using 3â5% water by weight of massecuite is a good balance between washing and yield.

quiz.q: What is affination?
options: A) Mixing raw sugar with heavy syrup to remove molasses film
B) Boiling sugar to high supersaturation
quiz.explanation: Affination softens and removes the molasses coating on raw sugar crystals.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of affination syrup?
quiz.explanation: Affination syrup (70â75 Brix) softens the molasses film so it can be washed off.

quiz.q: What temperature range is recommended for affination washing?
quiz.explanation: Water at 60â70Â°C effectively removes molasses without dissolving too much sugar.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of affination?
options: B) Reduces color and ash in raw sugar
quiz.explanation: Affination reduces color, ash, and impurities by 50â70%, improving sugar quality.

quiz.q: What is final molasses?
options: A) Molasses from the first strike
B) Molasses left after maximum sugar extraction
quiz.explanation: Final molasses is the heavy syrup remaining after all recoverable sugar is crystallized.

quiz.q: What is a common use of molasses in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Molasses is widely used as an energy-rich animal feed mixed with roughage.

quiz.q: How much ethanol can be produced from one tonne of molasses?
quiz.explanation: Fermentation of one tonne of molasses yields about 250â300 liters of ethanol.

quiz.q: What is a key parameter to control during molasses exhaustion?
quiz.explanation: Controlling supersaturation and temperature ensures maximum sugar crystallization from molasses.

quiz.q: What is crystal size distribution (CSD)?
options: A) The average size of crystals
B) The range of crystal sizes in a sample
quiz.explanation: CSD describes the spread of crystal sizes, indicating uniformity.

quiz.q: Why is uniform crystal size important?
options: B) It improves centrifugation and washing
quiz.explanation: Uniform crystals centrifuge and wash more efficiently, leading to better quality and yield.

quiz.q: How is CSD measured in a lab?
options: B) Using a set of sieves
quiz.explanation: Sieving separates crystals by size, and the fractions are weighed to determine distribution.

quiz.q: What is a typical moisture content for white sugar?
quiz.explanation: White sugar should have very low moisture, typically below 0.05%, to prevent caking.

quiz.q: What does ICUMSA measure?
quiz.explanation: ICUMSA units measure color; lower values indicate whiter sugar.

quiz.q: What is a simple field method to check crystal size?
options: A) Use a magnifier and ruler
quiz.explanation: A magnifier and ruler allow approximate measurement of crystal dimensions.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see many fine crystals in your sugar?
options: B) Reduce supersaturation or add more seed
quiz.explanation: Reducing supersaturation or adding seed helps control nucleation and reduce fines.
